title: 08. Microservices & Architecture Patterns: Kubernetes
summary: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates the deployment, scaling, networking, self-healing, and operational lifecycle of containerized applications across a cluster of machines —…

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform that automates the deployment, scaling, networking, self-healing, and operational lifecycle of containerized applications across a cluster of machines — abstracting compute resources into a declarative API of Pods, Deployments, Services, and related objects, with a control plane that continuously reconciles the cluster's actual state toward the declared desired state.

Once an organization has containerized its services (Docker), it faces a new problem: how to run those containers across many machines, keep them running when machines fail, scale them up and down with load, update them without downtime, and route traffic to them. Doing this manually — SSHing into machines, running `docker run`, hoping the container stays up — does not scale beyond a handful of machines and a few services. Kubernetes solves this by providing a declarative API: the operator describes the desired state (e.g., "run 3 replicas of the order service, expose it on port 80, scale to 10 replicas when CPU exceeds 70%"), and Kubernetes continuously works to make the cluster's actual state match the desired state. If a machine dies and takes 2 of the 3 order-service replicas with it, Kubernetes notices and schedules 2 new replicas on healthy machines — automatically, without operator intervention. If load spikes and CPU exceeds 70%, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adds replicas until CPU drops. If a new version is deployed, the rolling update replaces replicas one at a time, with a readiness check ensuring new replicas serve traffic before old ones are terminated. This automation is what makes Kubernetes the de facto standard for container orchestration.

The architecture has two planes. The **control plane** (master nodes) is the brain: the **API server** is the front door (all operations go through it, via `kubectl` or the REST API); the **etcd** key-value store is the source of truth for cluster state (a Raft-consensus distributed store, the only stateful component of the control plane); the **scheduler** decides which node each Pod runs on (based on resource requests, affinity rules, taints); the **controller manager** runs reconciliation loops (the Deployment controller ensures N replicas exist; the ReplicaSet controller creates Pods; the Node controller evicts Pods from dead nodes); the **cloud controller manager** integrates with the cloud provider (provisioning load balancers, persistent volumes). The **data plane** (worker nodes) is the muscle: each node runs the **kubelet** (an agent that talks to the API server, starts and stops containers via the container runtime), the **kube-proxy** (manages iptables/IPVS rules for Service networking), and a **container runtime** (containerd, CRI-O, or historically Docker). The control plane is the operator's interface; the data plane is where the workloads actually run. This separation lets the control plane manage thousands of nodes — it is a small set of stateless(ish) services, while the data plane scales horizontally with the workload.

The real-world journey that made Kubernetes dominant started at Google. Google had been running containers internally since 2003 with Borg (their internal orchestration system, described in a 2015 paper), and a second-generation system called Omega. Kubernetes (Greek for "helmsman," often shortened to K8s for the 8 letters between K and s) was open-sourced in 2014, designed by Google engineers (including Joe Beda, Brendan Burns, and Craig McLuckie) as a Borg-inspired but cloud-native, vendor-neutral orchestration platform. Google donated Kubernetes to the newly-formed Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) in 2015, and the project exploded: by 2018 it was the standard for container orchestration, with all major cloud providers offering managed Kubernetes (EKS on AWS, GKE on GCP, AKS on Azure). The watershed real-world validation was **Pokémon Go** (2016, Niantic). Niantic expected a popular launch but got a phenomenon — millions of concurrent players far exceeding their pre-launch capacity estimates. Their infrastructure was on Google Cloud and used Kubernetes for container orchestration; by rapidly scaling the cluster (adding nodes and replicas) they absorbed the load that would have crushed a static infrastructure. The story became the canonical "Kubernetes scales" case study. **Shopify** ran on Kubernetes at scale (handling Black Friday traffic), migrating from a traditional VM-based infrastructure to K8s over 2017–2019, running tens of thousands of Pods across multiple clusters. Both cases validated Kubernetes's core promise: declarative desired state, automatic reconciliation, horizontal scaling.

The trade-offs of Kubernetes are real and are often underappreciated by teams adopting it. **Operational complexity**: Kubernetes is a complex distributed system with dozens of resource types, hundreds of API options, and a steep learning curve. Operating it (especially self-hosted, not managed) requires deep expertise — etcd backups, control-plane HA, certificate management, network policy, RBAC. Managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS) reduce but do not eliminate this burden; you still operate the workloads. **Resource overhead**: the control plane consumes resources (etcd, API server, controllers), and each node's kubelet and kube-proxy add overhead. For very small workloads, this overhead exceeds the benefit — a single-service deployment on one VM is simpler and cheaper. **YAML sprawl**: a typical microservice deployment is dozens of YAML files (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA, PDB, NetworkPolicy), and managing this sprawl (with Helm, Kustomize, or GitOps tools like ArgoCD) is its own discipline. **Debugging complexity**: when a Pod fails to schedule or a Service does not route, the failure modes span many components (scheduler, kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime, network plugin), and debugging requires understanding all of them. **Vendor lock-in risk**: while Kubernetes itself is portable, the ecosystem (Ingress controllers, storage classes, cloud integrations) often couples you to a specific cloud or tooling.

The deeper lesson is that Kubernetes is an infrastructure platform, not an application framework — it solves the problem of running containers reliably across a cluster, but it does not solve application architecture, service-to-service communication (that is service mesh), or observability (that is tracing/metrics/logging). The teams that succeed with Kubernetes treat it as one layer in a stack: containers (Docker) at the bottom, Kubernetes orchestrating them, a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) handling inter-service communication, an observability stack (Prometheus, Jaeger, Loki) for monitoring, and a deployment tool (Helm, ArgoCD) for managing the YAML. The teams that struggle are usually the ones that expect Kubernetes alone to solve all their operational problems — it solves one (orchestration) very well, but the other layers are still your responsibility. For any organization running more than ~20 services or more than ~10 machines, Kubernetes (or a managed equivalent like ECS, Nomad) is the right orchestration layer; below that scale, simpler tools (Docker Compose, ECS, plain VMs) may suffice.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Picks a node for each pending pod (bin-packs by cpu_request).
- Reconciliation loop: actual state -> desired state.
- Watches CPU; scales deployment when threshold exceeded.
- Kubernetes scheduler + HPA mock: demonstrates reconciliation, pod placement,
- Readiness, service endpoints, and horizontal scaling on CPU metrics.
- Scale down (terminate excess, oldest first)

**Defines:** `Pod`, `Node`, `Deployment`, `Scheduler`, `Controller`, `HPA`, `simulate_load()`

```python
# Kubernetes scheduler + HPA mock: demonstrates reconciliation, pod placement,
# readiness, service endpoints, and horizontal scaling on CPU metrics.
import random, time, threading

class Pod:
    def __init__(self, name, image, cpu_request):
        self.name, self.image, self.cpu_request = name, image, cpu_request
        self.node = None
        self.ready = False
        self.cpu_usage = 0.0  # fraction of request
        self.status = "Pending"

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name, cpu_capacity):
        self.name = name
        self.cpu_capacity = cpu_capacity  # millicores, e.g. 4000 = 4 cores
        self.cpu_allocated = 0
        self.pods = []
    def can_fit(self, cpu_request):
        return self.cpu_allocated + cpu_request <= self.cpu_capacity

class Deployment:
    def __init__(self, name, image, replicas, cpu_request):
        self.name, self.image = name, image
        self.replicas, self.cpu_request = replicas, cpu_request
        self.pods = []

class Scheduler:
    """Picks a node for each pending pod (bin-packs by cpu_request)."""
    def schedule(self, pod, nodes):
        for n in nodes:  # first-fit; real K8s uses scoring (bin-packing, anti-affinity)
            if n.can_fit(pod.cpu_request):
                pod.node = n
                n.cpu_allocated += pod.cpu_request
                n.pods.append(pod)
                pod.status = "Running"
                return True
        return False

class Controller:
    """Reconciliation loop: actual state -> desired state."""
    def reconcile(self, deployment, nodes):
        ready = [p for p in deployment.pods if p.status != "Terminated"]
        # scale up
        while len(ready) < deployment.replicas:
            pod = Pod(f"{deployment.name}-{len(deployment.pods)+1}",
                      deployment.image, deployment.cpu_request)
            deployment.pods.append(pod)
            ready.append(pod)
            self._schedule_and_start(pod, nodes)
        # scale down (terminate excess, oldest first)
        while len(ready) > deployment.replicas:
            pod = ready.pop(0)
            pod.status = "Terminated"
            if pod.node:
                pod.node.cpu_allocated -= pod.cpu_request
                pod.node.pods.remove(pod)

    def _schedule_and_start(self, pod, nodes):
        sched = Scheduler()
        if sched.schedule(pod, nodes):
            time.sleep(0.05)  # simulate image pull + container start
            pod.ready = True  # readiness probe passes
            pod.cpu_usage = random.uniform(0.2, 0.5)

class HPA:
    """Watches CPU; scales deployment when threshold exceeded."""
    def __init__(self, target_cpu=0.7, min_replicas=1, max_replicas=10):
        self.target_cpu, self.min_r, self.max_r = target_cpu, min_replicas, max_replicas
    def evaluate(self, deployment, controller, nodes):
        ready = [p for p in deployment.pods if p.ready]
        if not ready:
            return
        avg_cpu = sum(p.cpu_usage for p in ready) / len(ready)
        if avg_cpu > self.target_cpu and deployment.replicas < self.max_r:
            deployment.replicas += 1
            print(f"[HPA] CPU {avg_cpu:.2f} > {self.target_cpu} -> "
                  f"scale to {deployment.replicas}")
            controller.reconcile(deployment, nodes)
        elif avg_cpu < self.target_cpu * 0.5 and deployment.replicas > self.min_r:
            deployment.replicas -= 1
            print(f"[HPA] CPU {avg_cpu:.2f} low -> scale to {deployment.replicas}")
            controller.reconcile(deployment, nodes)

def simulate_load(ready_pods, spike=False):
    for p in ready_pods:
        p.cpu_usage = min(0.95, p.cpu_usage + random.uniform(0.05, 0.4 if spike else 0.1))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    nodes = [Node("node-1", 4000), Node("node-2", 4000)]
    deploy = Deployment("order-svc", "order:v1", replicas=2, cpu_request=500)
    ctrl = Controller()
    ctrl.reconcile(deploy, nodes)
    hpa = HPA(target_cpu=0.7, min_replicas=1, max_replicas=6)
    for tick in range(8):
        ready = [p for p in deploy.pods if p.ready]
        simulate_load(ready, spike=(tick == 3))
        avg = sum(p.cpu_usage for p in ready) / len(ready) if ready else 0
        print(f"tick {tick}: replicas={len(ready)} avg_cpu={avg:.2f} "
              f"nodes={[ (n.name, n.cpu_allocated) for n in nodes]}")
        hpa.evaluate(deploy, ctrl, nodes)
        time.sleep(0.05)
    print(f"\nfinal pods: {[ (p.name, p.node.name if p.node else None, p.status) for p in deploy.pods]}")
```

quiz.explanation: Pod** is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — a co-located group of one or more containers that share network and storage namespaces, scheduled together on one node. Each Pod has its own IP address (in the pod network), and containers in the same Pod share that IP and can communicate via localhost.

quiz.explanation: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically scales the number of Pods in a Deployment (or ReplicaSet) based on observed metrics — most commonly CPU and memory, but also custom metrics (requests-per-second, queue depth) via the custom metrics API. The mechanism: the HPA controller runs a reconciliation loop (default: every 30 seconds).

So a new v2 Pod does not receive traffic until it is ready, and an old v1 Pod is not terminated (and removed from endpoints) until a replacement is ready.
